EU-ForDAM: correlation metrics, insect vs insect

Do the existing records carry information about the missing ones?

Published

October 19, 2026

Why these metrics

The thesis rests on one sentence: damage from different agents tends to fluctuate together, so the existing records carry information about the missing ones. The correlation metrics test that sentence, pair by pair, for all 43 single insects (903 pairs). Groups follow Table 1 of the 2025 EU-ForDAM paper (data/lookup/paper_hierarchy_2025.csv). Aggregate reporting codes (several insects lumped together, e.g. “borers on pine”) are left out here, because comparing a group with its own members says nothing new; they are used in the group-level correlations at the end. Each question below serves one objective:

Question Metric Objective
1. Does insect A have bad years when insect B does, in the same region? same-year r, within region the premise
2. Does that link hold in every country? r per country 1, gap-filling (links learnt in one country fill gaps in another)
3. Is it regional, or just years bad all over Europe? Does one come first? r after removing Europe-wide years; A this year vs B next year 3, drivers and anticipation
4. Do linked insects share feeding type or host tree? share of strong links within vs between groups 2, damage across agents and host trees

How r is measured. value1 only (value2 is the same damage in another unit). 0 = monitored, no damage; not reported = unknown, left out. Damage on a log(1 + x) scale, each region’s series compared with its own average, so a large and a small region count the same. Only region-years where both insects were recorded. The 95% range comes from resampling whole regions 999 times; a link is sure when the range excludes 0, strong when also r ≥ 0.3. As in the 2025 EU-ForDAM paper, the spruce bark-borer group of Czechia and Germany is counted as I. typographus.

The heatmap: every insect against every other

How to read it: each square is one pair of insects. Red = they have bad years together, blue = one is high when the other is low; the darker, the stronger. Strong colour = a sure link; faded = the 95% range includes 0, so it could be chance. Black boxes are the usable links (strong and the same in every country checked). Blank = recorded together too rarely to measure. Lines split the paper’s four level-1 groups. The red block in the top left is the borers on gymnosperms (bark and wood borers on spruce, pine and fir): that is where most of the shared signal sits.

The answer in one figure

verdict pairs share meaning
usable 28 3% strong, and holds in every country checked: lean on it
promising 52 6% strong, but only seen in one country: cannot check yet
unreliable 12 1% strong, but differs between countries: do not transfer
weak 102 11% sure but small (r < 0.3)
no link 592 66% no detectable link
not enough data 117 13% recorded together too rarely to measure

1 and 2: the links we can use

  • 28 pairs are usable: strong, and the same direction and similar size in every country where they are recorded together. These are what gap-filling can lean on.
  • 52 more are strong but seen in one country only; they may be real but cannot be checked yet. 12 are strong in one place and not in another.
  • Almost all are positive (bad years together). One clear negative: Pityokteines spp. with Pristiphora abietina.

3: regional or Europe-wide, and does one come first?

  • 21 of the 28 usable links stay strong after removing years that were bad all over Europe (open circles near the green dots). So most links are regional, not just shared European weather. Regional drivers (local drought, storms) are the likely cause and are what the driver data should test (objective 3).
  • In 22 of the 28 usable pairs, one insect’s bad year also tends to come before the other’s in the next year. This is weaker and less certain than the same-year link, but it is the first hint that damage can be anticipated from the records (outputs/tables/CM_pairs_verdict.csv, column lead).

4: feeding type matters, host tree adds little

pair measurable pairs strong links share strong usable
different broad groups 564 31 5% 9
same broad group 222 61 27% 19

Level-1 groups of the paper: borers / defoliators on gymnosperms / angiosperms. Pairs in the same level-1 group are about five times as likely to be strongly linked. Most usable links are among borers on gymnosperms (bark beetles on spruce and pine); most others are borers on gymnosperms with borers on angiosperms (oak Scolytus and Agrilus), or pine defoliators with each other. A permutation test confirms the group effect (p = 0.001); sharing the same level-2 host adds little beyond it.

5: does a link predict a country it has never seen?

The correlation tells us two insects move together where both are recorded. Gap-filling needs more: a link learnt in some countries must work in a country that never reported one of the insects. So we test exactly that.

How. For each pair (A, B) and each country where both are recorded: hide that country, learn how B follows A in the other countries, then guess B’s ups and downs in the hidden country from A alone. Compare with the simplest guess, “a normal year”. Skill = how much smaller the error is: 0 = no help, 0.1 = 10% smaller error, below 0 = the link learnt elsewhere misleads. Both directions (A → B and B → A) are pooled.

predictive pairs meaning
predicts well 32 skill >= 0.05 and helps in at least 3 of 4 hidden countries
predicts a little 78 skill > 0 and helps in at least half
no help 75 about as good as guessing a normal year
misleads 56 skill < -0.05: the link does not transfer and makes guesses worse
cannot test 662 recorded together in fewer than 2 countries
verdict predicts well predicts a little no help misleads
usable 20 8 0 0
unreliable 2 5 2 3
  • The correlation verdicts hold up. All 28 usable pairs help predict a country left out: 20 predict well, 8 a little, none mislead. Of the 12 unreliable pairs, 3 make guesses worse, which is exactly why they were flagged.
  • The gain from one partner insect is modest. For usable pairs the error is typically 11% smaller (range 2-26%), and still 8% after removing years bad all over Europe. The best: I. acuminatus with I. duplicatus, I. typographus with Pityokteines, I. sexdentatus with Phaenops cyanea (about 25%).
  • High correlation is not enough. I. typographus with Pityogenes chalcographus has the highest pooled r and a high pooled skill, but the link differs between countries (strong in DE and AT, not in IT or SK), so it is “unreliable”.
  • Most pairs cannot be tested (662 of 903): they are recorded together in only one country.

For gap-filling this means: one partner insect gives a modest but real gain, so the factor model, which combines all partners at once, is the right tool. The usable links are the ones it can trust across countries.

Check: does the choice of correlation matter? (Spearman)

Pearson r uses the actual sizes of the ups and downs, so one huge outbreak year can dominate a series. Spearman r uses only the order of the years (which year was a region’s worst, second worst, …), so outbreaks cannot dominate. We reran the whole pipeline with within-region ranks instead of values.

  • The two agree almost perfectly: correlation between Pearson and Spearman r across all pairs = 0.97; typical difference 0.02.
  • Usable pairs: 28 with Pearson, 29 with Spearman, 22 in both. The pairs that switch sit right at the edges (r near 0.3, or consistent in one country check but not the other).
  • So the results are not driven by a few extreme outbreak years. Pearson stays the main metric; Spearman is the robustness check (outputs/tables/CM_pearson_vs_spearman.csv).

The paper’s groups (levels 1 and 2)

Group value in a region-year = sum of all recorded member codes, aggregates included. Same metric as above (within region, 95% range from resampling regions), plus the paper’s own approach (Pearson r of the Europe-wide yearly totals).

level2 Defoliators on P. abies Defoliators on P. sylvestris 619 0.35 0.25 to 0.46 0.54
  • Borers on spruce, pine and fir have bad years together; so do spruce and pine defoliators.
  • Borers and defoliators do not move together; borers on fir go against defoliators on spruce (the group version of the Pityokteines x Pristiphora link).
  • Europe-wide totals give much higher r than within-region series, because a Europe-wide total mixes regional signals with shared bad years; the within-region number is the one that matters for gap-filling.

What it means for the thesis

  1. The premise holds for a core of insects, not for all. About 12% of measurable pairs are strongly linked, mostly within feeding groups. For those insects, the records of one do carry information about the other.
  2. Gap-filling (objective 1) should lean on the 28 usable links and treat the rest with caution. The factor model does this automatically: it learns the shared patterns from all insects at once.
  3. Drivers and anticipation (objective 3): most links are regional, not Europe-wide, and some insects lead others by a year. Both point to regional drivers worth testing once the drought and storm data are in.
  4. Limit: many links can only be seen in one or two countries (mostly DE and CZ). More countries reporting more insects is what would firm this up.
